title: Authorizing a Custom Zscaler Connector for Microsoft Applications

blocks.text: The Zscaler service supports custom, client-side connector onboarding for access to the following Microsoft applications: Exchange, Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) Labels, OneDrive, SharePoint, Microsoft Azure Blob Storage, Teams, Dynamics 365, Copilot, and Microsoft 365. With this functionality, instead of requiring full administrator credentials, the Zscaler service can use a minimum set of credentials to access your Microsoft applications.

When you create a custom connector for a Microsoft application, you have the option to choose whether you want to provide a client secret or a private key in the Zscaler Admin Console so that the Zscaler service can access the application. Choosing the client secret option requires you to provide your Client ID, Client Secret, and Tenant ID. Choosing the private key option requires the Client ID, Tenant ID, and the Private Key PEM file.
Microsoft Purview Information Protection (MIP), SharePoint, Copilot, and Microsoft 365 require the private key method for onboarding; the client secret method is not available.
To create a custom connector for a Microsoft application:

blocks.item: 1. Create the custom connector.
This section covers how to register your Internet & SaaS (ZIA) API client application in Microsoft Entra ID and configure the client credentials.
Zscaler recommends creating a new connector for each Microsoft application to ensure isolation and better management.
Sign in to Azure portal.
In the Azure Services section, click App registrations.
The App registrations page is displayed.
Click New registration.
See image.
The Register an application window opens.
In the Register an application window:
Name: Enter a name for the application that is representative of the Zscaler connection you are creating (e.g., Zscaler OneDrive Connector).
Supported account types: Ensure that this option is set to the Accounts in any organizational directory (Any Microsoft Entra ID tenant - Multitenant) value.
Redirect URI (optional): Select Web as the platform, then provide the URL of the Zscaler account (e.g., https://console.zscaler.com/). Save the URL for later use.
See image.
Click Register.
The application is registered and the application's Overview page is displayed. Copy the Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID values from the Overview page and save them for later use.
See image.
2. Choose one of the following options to provide Zscaler access to the application:
Create client secret.
This section covers how to generate your client secret for use when authorizing the custom connector with Internet & SaaS.
Go to Certificates & secrets in the left-side navigation of the app and then click New client secret on the Client secrets tab.
See image.
The Add a client secret pane opens.
In the Add a client secret pane:
Description: Provide information about the client's secret.
Expires: Select the appropriate expiration time from the drop-down menu.
See image.
Click Add.
The client secret value is generated and displayed.
Copy the secret value immediately and save it for later use.
The client secret value is displayed only once and cannot be retrieved after you navigate away from the page.
See image.
Create private key.
This section covers how to generate your private key PEM file for authorizing the custom connector with Internet & SaaS using either Windows or Mac instructions.
Windows
a. Generate a certificate, private key, and combined PEM file.
For additional information about the files you need to create, refer to the following table:

table: Combined PEM file containing the private key and certificate
Upload on Internet & SaaS onboarding page.

blocks.item: To generate a certificate on a Windows device, copy the following code and run the commands using OpenSSL:

<# .SYNOPSIS Generate an AES-256 encrypted RSA private key + self-signed certificate, then bundle them into combined.pem. Compatible with OpenSSL 1.1.1 and 3.x. .NOTES Fixes vs. original: - Auto-resolves openssl.exe (param -> PATH -> Git mingw64 -> Win64). - Removes $ErrorActionPreference='Stop' (misfires on native stderr in PS 5.1); relies on explicit $LASTEXITCODE checks instead. - Prompts for the passphrase ONCE and passes it via an env var to every openssl call (-pass / -passin env:PW) so there are no repeated/interactive passphrase prompts and no stderr-prompt fragility. - MSYS path-conversion guards so -subj is never mangled. #> [CmdletBinding()] param( [string]$OpenSSL = '', # leave blank to auto-detect [string]$WorkingDir = "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads", [int] $Days = 0, [string]$Subject = '', # e.g. /C=US/ST=State/L=City/O=Org/CN=example.com [string]$Passphrase = '', # non-interactive/automation only; omit for secure prompt [switch]$EnableLog, # OFF by default. Pass -EnableLog to write a debug log file. [string]$LogFile = '', # optional custom log path; defaults to <WorkingDir>\New-CombinedPem.log [version]$MinVersion = '3.0.0' # minimum supported OpenSSL; the script refuses to run below this ) Set-StrictMode -Version Latest # Do NOT use 'Stop' around native exes on PS 5.1 — openssl's stderr prompts # can be promoted to terminating errors. We check $LASTEXITCODE explicitly. $ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue' # Guard the MSYS/mingw runtime against mangling POSIX-looking args (e.g. -subj). $env:MSYS_NO_PATHCONV = '1' $env:MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL = '*' # ---- Optional debug logging (opt-in via -EnableLog) -------------------------- # When -EnableLog is NOT supplied, Write-Log is a no-op: no file is created and # nothing is written. Secrets (passphrase) are never logged. if ($EnableLog -and -not $LogFile) { $LogFile = Join-Path $WorkingDir 'New-CombinedPem.log' } function Write-Log { param([string]$Message, [string]$Level = 'INFO') if (-not $EnableLog) { return } try { $dir = Split-Path -Parent $LogFile if ($dir -and -not (Test-Path $dir)) { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $dir -Force | Out-Null } $line = '{0} [{1}] {2}' -f (Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss'), $Level, $Message Add-Content -Path $LogFile -Value $line -Encoding UTF8 } catch { } # logging must never break the actual work } Write-Log ("=== New-CombinedPem started | PS {0} | {1} ===" -f $PSVersionTable.PSVersion, [Environment]::OSVersion.VersionString) if ($EnableLog) { Write-Host "Debug log: $LogFile" } function Resolve-OpenSSL { param([string]$Preferred) $candidates = @( $Preferred, (Get-Command openssl -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Source -First 1), 'C:\Program Files\OpenSSL-Win64\bin\openssl.exe', 'C:\Program Files\Git\mingw64\bin\openssl.exe' ) foreach ($c in $candidates) { if ($c -and (Test-Path -Path $c)) { return $c } } return $null } $OpenSSL = Resolve-OpenSSL -Preferred $OpenSSL if (-not $OpenSSL) { Write-Log 'OpenSSL not found on this machine.' 'ERROR' Write-Error "OpenSSL not found. Install it or pass -OpenSSL 'C:\path\to\openssl.exe'." exit 1 } Write-Host "Using OpenSSL: $OpenSSL" Write-Log "OpenSSL resolved: $OpenSSL" $verLine = (& $OpenSSL version) | Select-Object -First 1 if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or -not $verLine) { Write-Log "OpenSSL failed to run (exit $LASTEXITCODE)." 'ERROR' Write-Error "OpenSSL failed to run."; exit 1 } Write-Host "Detected: $verLine" # Enforce a minimum OpenSSL version. At >= 3.0.0 the modern `genpkey` path is # always available, so no legacy branching is needed. LibreSSL is not supported. if ($verLine -match 'LibreSSL') { Write-Log "Unsupported toolkit: $verLine" 'ERROR' Write-Error "LibreSSL is not supported. Use OpenSSL $MinVersion or newer."; exit 1 } if ($verLine -notmatch 'OpenSSL\s+(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)') { Write-Log "Could not parse OpenSSL version from: $verLine" 'ERROR' Write-Error "Could not determine OpenSSL version from '$verLine'."; exit 1 } $detected = [version]("{0}.{1}.{2}" -f $Matches[1], $Matches[2], $Matches[3]) if ($detected -lt $MinVersion) { Write-Log "OpenSSL $detected is below the minimum required ($MinVersion)." 'ERROR' Write-Error "OpenSSL $detected found, but $MinVersion or newer is required."; exit 1 } Write-Host "Version OK: $detected (>= $MinVersion)" Write-Log "Version: $verLine | detected $detected (min $MinVersion)" # ---- Paths ------------------------------------------------------------------- if (-not (Test-Path -Path $WorkingDir)) { New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $WorkingDir -Force | Out-Null } $EncryptedKey = Join-Path $WorkingDir 'private_key.pem' $Certificate = Join-Path $WorkingDir 'certificate.pem' $CombinedPEM = Join-Path $WorkingDir 'combined.pem' # ---- Validity days ----------------------------------------------------------- if ($Days -le 0) { $daysInput = Read-Host 'Enter certificate validity in days (e.g. 365)' if (-not [int]::TryParse($daysInput, [ref]$Days) -or $Days -le 0) { Write-Error 'Invalid days value. Must be a positive integer.'; exit 1 } } # ---- Passphrase -------------------------------------------------------------- if ($Passphrase) { # Non-interactive path (automation/CI). Passphrase supplied by caller. if ($Passphrase.Length -lt 4) { Write-Error 'Passphrase too short (min 4 chars).'; exit 1 } $env:PW = $Passphrase } else { # Secure interactive path: prompt once, with confirmation. $sec1 = Read-Host 'Enter a passphrase for the private key' -AsSecureString $sec2 = Read-Host 'Confirm passphrase' -AsSecureString $b1 = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($sec1) $b2 = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($sec2) try { $p1 = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringBSTR($b1) $p2 = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringBSTR($b2) if ($p1 -ne $p2) { Write-Error 'Passphrases do not match.'; exit 1 } if ($p1.Length -lt 4) { Write-Error 'Passphrase too short (min 4 chars).'; exit 1 } $env:PW = $p1 } finally { [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ZeroFreeBSTR($b1) [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ZeroFreeBSTR($b2) } } Write-Log ("Run params | WorkingDir: {0} | Days: {1} | Subject: {2}" -f $WorkingDir, $Days, ($(if ($Subject) { $Subject } else { '(interactive)' }))) try { # ---- Step 1: encrypted RSA private key ---------------------------------- # OpenSSL >= 3.0.0 (enforced above) always supports genpkey with -pass. Write-Host "`n[1/4] Generating AES-256 encrypted RSA private key (genpkey)..." & $OpenSSL genpkey -algorithm RSA -aes256 -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048 ` -pass env:PW -out "$EncryptedKey" if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or -not (Test-Path $EncryptedKey)) { Write-Log "Step 1 FAILED: key not generated (openssl exit $LASTEXITCODE)." 'ERROR' Write-Error 'Failed to generate encrypted private key.'; exit 1 } Write-Host " OK -> $EncryptedKey" Write-Log 'Step 1 OK: private_key.pem generated.' # ---- Step 2: self-signed certificate ------------------------------------ # `req` needs an openssl.cnf. Some builds (portable zips, relocated installs) # have a compiled-in config path that doesn't exist -> req fails. We try the # build's own config first, then transparently retry with a generated # minimal config so the script works regardless of how OpenSSL was deployed. Write-Host "`n[2/4] Creating self-signed certificate..." $reqArgs = @('req','-new','-x509','-key',"$EncryptedKey",'-passin','env:PW','-days',"$Days",'-out',"$Certificate") if (-not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($Subject)) { $reqArgs += @('-subj',"$Subject") } & $OpenSSL @reqArgs if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or -not (Test-Path $Certificate)) { Write-Host ' (default config unavailable; retrying with a generated minimal config)' Write-Log "Step 2: default openssl.cnf unavailable (exit $LASTEXITCODE); using generated minimal config." 'WARN' $fallbackCnf = Join-Path $WorkingDir '_min_openssl.cnf' # A complete req template so BOTH modes work when the build has no config: # - with -subj : the subject overrides these prompts (no interaction) # - without -subj: OpenSSL prompts interactively for each DN field below $minCnf = @" [ req ] distinguished_name = req_dn prompt = yes [ req_dn ] countryName = Country Name (2 letter code) countryName_default = US countryName_min = 2 countryName_max = 2 stateOrProvinceName = State or Province Name localityName = Locality Name 0.organizationName = Organization Name organizationalUnitName = Organizational Unit Name commonName = Common Name (e.g. server FQDN) commonName_max = 64 emailAddress = Email Address emailAddress_max = 64 "@ Set-Content -Path $fallbackCnf -Value $minCnf -Encoding ascii $savedConf = if (Test-Path Env:\OPENSSL_CONF) { $env:OPENSSL_CONF } else { $null } $env:OPENSSL_CONF = $fallbackCnf try { & $OpenSSL @reqArgs } finally { if ($null -ne $savedConf) { $env:OPENSSL_CONF = $savedConf } else { Remove-Item Env:\OPENSSL_CONF -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue } } if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or -not (Test-Path $Certificate)) { Write-Log "Step 2 FAILED: certificate not created even with fallback config (exit $LASTEXITCODE)." 'ERROR' Write-Error 'Failed to create certificate.'; exit 1 } } Write-Host " OK -> $Certificate" Write-Log 'Step 2 OK: certificate.pem created.' # ---- Step 3: combine (byte-level, like `cat`) --------------------------- Write-Host "`n[3/4] Combining key + certificate into combined PEM..." $keyBytes = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes($EncryptedKey) $certBytes = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllBytes($Certificate) [System.IO.File]::WriteAllBytes($CombinedPEM, $keyBytes + $certBytes) Write-Host " OK -> $CombinedPEM" Write-Log ("Step 3 OK: combined.pem written ({0} bytes = {1} key + {2} cert)." -f ($keyBytes.Length + $certBytes.Length), $keyBytes.Length, $certBytes.Length) # ---- Step 4: verify (works across all versions & key formats) ----------- Write-Host "`n[4/4] Verifying..." Write-Host (" Key header : {0}" -f (Get-Content $EncryptedKey -First 1)) # Confirm the key is genuinely encrypted AND the passphrase unlocks it. & $OpenSSL pkey -in "$EncryptedKey" -passin env:PW -noout 2>$null if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { Write-Host ' Key check : passphrase unlocks the encrypted key (OK)'; Write-Log 'Step 4 OK: passphrase unlocks the encrypted key.' } else { Write-Host ' Key check : could not verify key (non-fatal)'; Write-Log 'Step 4 WARN: key unlock check inconclusive (non-fatal).' 'WARN' } & $OpenSSL x509 -in "$Certificate" -noout -subject -enddate Write-Host "`nDone. Combined PEM: $CombinedPEM" Write-Log "=== Completed successfully. Output: $CombinedPEM ===" } finally { # Always scrub the passphrase from the environment. Remove-Item Env:\PW -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue }
b. Upload the certificate file to the created client connector.
In the Azure portal, go to App registrations and click on the client connector you created. In the left-side navigation, go to Manage > Certificates & secrets.
See image.
Click the Certificates tab and then click Upload certificate.
See image.
In the Description field, enter a description for the certificate.
Upload the public certificate PEM file and click Add.
Mac
a. Generate a certificate, private key, and combined PEM file.
For additional information about the files you need to create, refer to the following table:

table: Combined PEM file containing the private key and certificate
Upload on Internet & SaaS onboarding page.

blocks.item: To generate a certificate on a Mac device, copy the following code and run the commands using OpenSSL:

#!/bin/bash set -e # Exit the script if any command fails # Prompt for missing values read_if_missing() { local varname="$1"; local prompt="$2"; local default="${3:-}" if [[ -z "${!varname:-}" ]]; then if [[ -n "$default" ]]; then read -rp "$prompt [$default]: " val val="${val:-$default}" else read -rp "$prompt: " val fi printf -v "$varname" '%s' "$val" fi } read_if_missing DAYS "Certificate validity in days" "$DAYS" # File definitions ENCRYPTED_PRIVATE_KEY="private_key.pem" # AES-encrypted private key CERTIFICATE="certificate.pem" # Self-signed certificate COMBINED_PEM="combined.pem" # Final combined PEM file # Step 1: Generate an AES-encrypted RSA private key echo "🔐 Generating an AES-256 encrypted RSA private key..." openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -aes256 -out "$ENCRYPTED_PRIVATE_KEY" -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048 if [[ $? -ne 0 ]]; then echo "❌ Failed to generate AES-encrypted private key." exit 1 fi echo "✅ Successfully created AES-encrypted private key: '$ENCRYPTED_PRIVATE_KEY'." # Step 2: Create a self-signed certificate using the encrypted private key echo "📜 Generating a self-signed certificate..." openssl req -new -x509 -key "$ENCRYPTED_PRIVATE_KEY" -out "$CERTIFICATE" -days $DAYS if [[ $? -ne 0 ]]; then echo "❌ Failed to create certificate." exit 1 fi echo "✅ Successfully created self-signed certificate: '$CERTIFICATE'." # Step 3: Combine encrypted private key and certificate into a single PEM file echo "📦 Combining encrypted private key and certificate into '$COMBINED_PEM'..." cat "$ENCRYPTED_PRIVATE_KEY" "$CERTIFICATE" > "$COMBINED_PEM" if [[ $? -ne 0 ]]; then echo "❌ Failed to combine files into PEM." exit 1 fi echo "✅ Successfully created combined PEM file: '$COMBINED_PEM'." # Step 5: Confirm Encryption Details in the Encrypted Key echo "🔍 Confirming encryption type used in the private key..." openssl asn1parse -in "$ENCRYPTED_PRIVATE_KEY" echo "🎉 All steps completed successfully! The combined PEM file is located at '$COMBINED_PEM'."
b. Upload the certificate file to the created client connector.
In the Azure portal, go to App registrations and click on the client connector you created. In the left-side navigation, go to Manage > Certificates & secrets.
See image.
Click the Certificates tab and then click Upload certificate.
See image.
In the Description field, enter a description for the certificate.
Upload the public certificate PEM file and click Add.
For information on which Microsoft applications currently support client secret or private key onboarding, refer to the following table:

table: Custom Connector (via Client ID and Secret)

blocks.item: 3. Generate API permissions for the connector.
You must assign specific API permissions for each Microsoft connector you create for the Zscaler service.
Go to API permissions in the left-side navigation and then click Add a permission under Configured permissions.
The Request API permissions pane is displayed.
See image.
On the Microsoft APIs tab, click an API to assign permissions (i.e., Microsoft Graph). To learn more, see the complete list of API permissions.
Click Application permissions.
See image.
In the Select permissions list, select each necessary permission for the connector.
Click Add permissions.
See image.
The permissions appear in the Configured permissions list on the API permissions page.
See image.
If admin consent is required (such as SharePoint permissions), select Grant admin consent.
In the Grant admin consent confirmation window, select Yes.
4. Add role assignments (for Microsoft Azure Blob Storage only).
If you are setting up a custom connector for Microsoft Azure Blob Storage, you must add additional role assignments in Azure to ensure that the Zscaler service can properly access the application.
Go to Azure Services > Enterprise Applications.
See image.
Copy the Tenant ID and the Application name matching the ID from when you created the custom connector and client secret.
See image.
Go back to the Azure portal home page, then go to Subscriptions and select your subscription.
See image.
Go to Access Control (IAM) > Role Assignments > Add > Add role assignment.
See image.
Search Storage Contributor. Select Storage Blob Data Contributor and Storage Account Contributor and then click Next. You must do this separately for each role.
Click Select members and add the application as a member to Storage Blob Data Contributor and Storage Account Contributor, then select Review + assign.
See image.
5. Authorize the custom connector.

To authorize a custom connector, you must first manually update the Azure login URL to grant permissions for the application on the tenant. After that, you must provide the Client ID, Client Secret, and Tenant ID in the Zscaler Admin Console so that the Zscaler service can access the application. You can create custom connectors for Microsoft SaaS application tenants or for MIP accounts.
Creating a Custom Connector for a SaaS Application Tenant
In the Zscaler Admin Console, from the navigation menu, go to Data Security > DSPM > SaaS Application Tenants.
Click Add SaaS Application Tenant.
The Add SaaS Application Tenant page is displayed.
Under Choose the SaaS Application Provider, select a Microsoft SaaS application.
In the Tenant Name field, provide a name.
Copy one of the following URLs and paste it in a separate browser tab:
For Microsoft 365 and Microsoft 365 GCC tenants: https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/adminconsent?client_id=<client_id>&state=administration/add-casb-tenants&redirect_uri=<redirect_uri>
For Microsoft 365 GCC High and Microsoft 365 DoD tenants: https://login.microsoftonline.us/common/adminconsent?client_id=<client_id>&state=administration/add-casb-tenants&redirect_uri=<redirect_uri>
In the URL, replace the client_id parameter with the Application (client) ID that you copied earlier, and replace the redirect_uri with the Redirect URI that you copied earlier.
Press Enter on your keyboard.
A Microsoft window appears listing the permissions requested by the Zscaler service.
See image.
Click Accept.
You return to the Add SaaS Application Tenant page.
In the Authorize the SaaS Application section, select Custom for the SaaS Connector.
Select whether you want to connect your app with Zscaler using the Client Secret or the Private Key.
See image.
If you select Client Secret, enter the values for the Client ID, Client Secret, and Tenant ID that you copied earlier.
See image.
If you select Private Key, enter the values you copied earlier for the Client ID and Tenant ID and click Upload PEM File to upload the file you created earlier. Enter your password when prompted.
See image.
Click Authorize.
If you're onboarding Copilot, copy the Zscaler SaaS Connector for use in the next section.
In the Zscaler Admin Console, click Save and activate the change.

After adding the tenants, you can configure the Data at Rest Scanning DLP policy, Malware Detection policy, and Scan Configuration. You can also view reports and data for the tenants in the SaaS Security Report, Insights, and Logs.
Creating a Custom Connector for an MIP Account
In the Zscaler Admin Console, from the navigation menu, go to Data Security > Common Resources > MIP Labels.
On the Microsoft Information Protection (MIP) Labels page, click Add MIP Account.
The Add MIP Account window appears.
See image.
Copy one of the following URLs and paste it in a separate browser tab:
For Microsoft 365 and Microsoft 365 GCC tenants: https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/adminconsent?client_id=<client_id>&state=administration/mip-labels&redirect_uri=<redirect_uri>
For Microsoft 365 GCC High and Microsoft 365 DoD tenants: https://login.microsoftonline.us/common/adminconsent?client_id=<client_id>&state=administration/mip-labels&redirect_uri=<redirect_uri>
In the URL, replace the client_id parameter with the Application (client) ID that you copied earlier, and replace the redirect_uri with the Redirect URI that you copied earlier.
Press Enter on your keyboard.
A Microsoft window appears listing the permissions requested by the Zscaler service.
See image.
Click Accept.
Return to the Add MIP Account window.
Select Custom for the SaaS Connector.
Enter the values for the Client ID, Client Secret, and Tenant ID that you copied earlier, then click Validate.
See image.
The Add MIP Account window reappears, displaying the next window for account details.
See image.
In the Add MIP Account window, under Account Name, enter a name you want to associate with the Microsoft account. It must be unique.
Click Save and activate the change.

The MIP account is added to the Zscaler Admin Console. The MIP Account displays a status of Validation Successful if the account is authorized. It displays a status of Validation Failed if the account is not authorized. If the status on the MIP account is Validation Failed, you can try the authorization process again by clicking Reauthorize on the Edit MIP Account window.
Change the Label Retrieval field for the MIP account.
6. Register application for admin management (Microsoft Copilot only).

To complete the app registration for Copilot, run the following script in Azure via Power Platform API or PowerShell for Power Platform administrators. Use the Zscaler Connector ID you copied earlier:

$appId = "<Zscaler Connector ID>" # Login interactively with a tenant administrator for Power Platform Add-PowerAppsAccount -Endpoint prod -TenantID $tenantId # Register a new application, this gives the SPN/client application the same permissions New-PowerAppManagementApp -ApplicationId $appId

blocks.text: When creating custom connectors, provide the following application-specific API permissions to ensure that the Zscaler service has the access it needs.

blocks.item: API Permissions for Microsoft Applications

In the following API tables, you need to select a different application from the Request API permissions page for each row of the Microsoft API column. For example, Azure requires selecting the same user_impersonation permission for both Azure Storage and Windows Azure Service Management.

Microsoft 365
Copilot
Exchange
Microsoft Azure Blob Storage
Microsoft Information Protection (MIP)
